title: Hercules Cleans the Augean Stables
text:
For his fifth labor, King Eurystheus ordered Hercules to carry out all the dung from the cattle yards of Augeas, king of Elis, in a single day. Augeas owned enormous herds, and the filth had piled up for years. It was a task meant to be both impossible and humiliating.

Hercules went to Augeas without mentioning that he was acting on Eurystheus's orders. He offered to clear out all the dung in one day in return for a tenth of the king's cattle. Augeas did not believe it could be done and agreed, and his son Phyleus witnessed the promise.

Hercules did not pick up a shovel. Two rivers, the Alpheus and the Peneus, flowed nearby. He broke an opening through the foundations of the cattle yard, cut channels to turn both rivers into it, and made another opening on the far side for the water to flow out. The torrent swept through and carried all the filth away.

Augeas then learned that the work had been ordered by Eurystheus and refused to pay, denying he had ever promised anything. When the dispute came before judges, Phyleus testified against his own father, and Augeas angrily banished them both. Eurystheus, for his part, refused to count the labor, because Hercules had done it for pay.
lesson: When a job looks impossible by hand, look for a larger force already flowing nearby that you can redirect. And get agreements in a form that will hold when the other side wants out.
date: Greek myth; Apollodorus, 1st or 2nd century AD
caveat: Other ancient authors tell the story with different details.
